items.title: A bust-up between mathematicians is fuelling fears that AI could undermine science
items.summary: AI has made some awesome scientific discoveries. But now, questions are being raised about its accuracy
items.content:
A bank of white freezers hums away at a former watch factory in central London. Inside: dozens of small boxes with barcoded glass tubes, collectively containing one hundred billion genes. Just two boxes may hold 10 times more information than all the text on the internet, says Dr Oliver Vince, the facility's co-founder.

His firm, Basecamp Research, plans to collect as much DNA as possible to create an artificial intelligence that can speak the language of biology, in the same way that US and Chinese tech firms have hoovered up written material online to create Large Language Models (LLMs), the basis of current AI systems.

Vince, like many in business and academic research, believes AI will supercharge scientific research. But increasingly, it also comes with controversy.

Last month, OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, said it had solved one of maths' great unsolved problems, relating to the famous Navier–Stokes equations. The company said its AI agents had cracked it in 88 hours. The body that runs a prize for whoever can solve the problem said it had "apparently been settled", but that its review would take time.

But hours before the announcement, Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University, went public with concerns. He formed an independent team with Levent Alpöge, a mathematician employed by day by the rival company Anthropic.

They had been working towards the same goal, and kept their drafts in OpenAI's coding tool, Codex. Buckmaster said that his co-researcher was tipped off that news of their progress had "reached" OpenAI, though he did not specify how. He asked whether his research, stored in Codex, could have fed into OpenAI's own work, though he stressed he was "not accusing anyone of anything".

OpenAI said that nobody at the company, human or AI, saw the other teams' work before it was published. Initially it said that while unlikely, it could not "rule out" that anonymised data from use of its products may have helped improve its models. Days later, it said Buckmaster's Codex prompts from the two months before the announcement "could not have influenced the system in any way".

It's a complicated story; we still don't fully know what happened. But it highlights a growing issue about the use of AI in science. Usually, those words make us conjure up images of robots building terrible genetically-engineered viruses, or chemical weapons, to wipe out humanity. But there's a more subtle problem that hasn't attracted the same headline-grabbing attention: that AI could undermine faith in the scientific process, raising questions about the novelty and accuracy of research.

And there's another concern. It's well known that AI chatbots like Claude or Gemini can sometimes hallucinate things that simply aren't true. They will tell you about a film that never existed, or a quote that was never said. Now there is evidence that this is increasingly happening in science. Eventually, it's feared, it will become difficult to separate true scientific discovery from AI-generated fiction.

And all of this could threaten to erode - if not explode - the rock on which scientific research rests: trust.

One threat is to scientific journals, the guardians of scientific integrity, which are seen to be failing to deal with a tsunami of AI-generated distortions.

"Generative AI has basically disrupted the whole scientific process," says Dalmeet Singh Chawla, a science journalist who has spent a decade reporting on research misconduct.

He tells the BBC that publishers' integrity staff - the people who screen submissions for accuracy and reliability - will need to "drastically increase [in number and effort] if they're anywhere near the fight". He says: "Right now, it seems like they're not."

On the face of it, AI seems just the right tool to power scientific research. Scientists deal with huge amounts of information. Telescopes and particle accelerators, for example, collect billions of data points – too large for the brain to comprehend. AI can pick the scientific highlights from the surrounding humdrum.

The poster child of scientific AI is the UK-based firm Google DeepMind, which in 2020 solved one of biology's biggest problems: how proteins in living things fold into their precise shapes.

It may sound dull, but proteins are the tiny machines that make life work, and the shapes they fold into determine what they can do; from building cells and fighting infection to helping form the tissues and organs of the body.

Before AI, scientists had to conduct time-consuming experiments in the lab. Then, Google DeepMind developed an AI model called AlphaFold that accurately predicted 200 million protein folds in just one year.

The equivalent experimental work would have taken hundreds of millions of years in laboratories. The firm gave the results away for free to researchers. The head of DeepMind and the project's lead scientist were both awarded the Nobel Prize for Chemistry.

Dr Pushmeet Kohli, who leads DeepMind's science work, told me that AlphaFold could be seen as a "watershed moment".

But elsewhere, the use of AI in science has come with accusations of hype. Some computer models are accused of exaggerating the significance of their findings, with the human researchers that oversee them then believing some of the claims without enough scepticism.

Basking in its success over AlphaFold, for example, DeepMind turned its attention to predicting the structure of new materials. The work could lead to the development of better batteries, cheaper solar cells and electronic components that are not dependent on rare earth elements. (In theory, no-one would need to argue about mining rights ever again, and Greenland would be safe from invasion.)

A DeepMind model came up with what the firm claimed were more than two million new crystal structures, announced as "nearly 800 years worth of knowledge" released in one go. Of those, some 380,000 were considered promising enough to make in a laboratory.

But then came a warning sign from two chemists at the University of California. Anthony Cheetham and Ram Seshadri went through a random sample of the supposed new crystals. Writing in the journal Chemistry of Materials, they concluded that they had "yet to find any strikingly novel compounds", arguing that many were "trivial adaptations of known materials". Their verdict was not that the method was wrong, but that the results need more scrutiny and validation from human chemists.

DeepMind rejects the charge, saying it tested each compound for novelty. Dismissing a new structure for looking familiar misses the point, the company argues: swapping a single atom is how many of today's most useful materials arrived, from phone components to sunscreen.

In those cases, at least, the science was mostly real and the issue was just AI potentially exaggerating its importance.

Arguably of even greater concern is the growing risk that scientific journals will become polluted with so-called AI "slop" - where a computer, not a human scientist, is writing the research, leading to fake citations and phantom papers.

In 2024, computer scientist Prof Dmitry Kobak, of Ghent University, searched more than a million biomedical research papers for trigger words favoured by the LLMs that generate AI writing. His team found that by December last year, nearly 90% had AI fingerprints on them. AI detection technology is not perfect; some forms of the software have labelled the US Constitution, written in the 1780s, as "AI-generated". But still, Kobak said he was shocked by the scale of apparent AI use. There is a risk, he told Nature, that "whatever bias the LLM may have will just suddenly permeate the (scientific) literature".

Kobak is among many researchers who worries that AI is slowly killing scientific journals.

And it matters: research papers are the lifeblood of scientific advance. When a discovery is published, another team in another part of the world might obtain funding to build on the results.

The process of peer review - in which research papers are checked by other scientists before they are published - is also being compromised.

A team led by Weixin Liang and James Zou at Stanford University analysed referee reports submitted to four major computer science conferences, and found up to 17% of the text had been substantially modified by a language model.

A critical part of a scientific paper's integrity involves lead scientists listing earlier research in order to show what they have done is genuinely new. These are called citations. A separate team at Cornell University found that researchers were using AI to compile citations, and that it was inventing bogus research, with around 147,000 pieces of phantom research cited last year.

If AI continues to distort the integrity of the academic process in this way, then researchers will be sent up blind alleys, public money will be wasted, and the fruits of valid research - such as new drugs or green technologies - will be slowed or not realised at all.

Some publishers of scientific journals, such as Elsevier, are taking steps to avert this growing crisis of confidence.

Il leader dem Golan: “Abbiamo l’opportunità di formare un governo con gli arabi”. Il capo della Lista Unita araba: “Chi vuole un’alternativa a Netanyahu dovrà parlare con noi”
items.content:
Eisenkot al premier: “Leader degno si sarebbe dimesso”. Netanyahu festeggia ma, allo stesso tempo, dice di rimanere in attesa dei risultati finali. All’86% dello scrutinio, 53 seggi andrebbero al blocco di Netanyahu, 48 a quello di Eisenkot, 19 ai partiti arabi.

Netanyahu: “Non permetteremo una coalizione con i partiti arabi”

Il capo della Lista Unita araba: “Chi vuole un’alternativa a Netanyahu dovrà parlare con noi”

Scrutinio al 76,8%: 54 seggi per il blocco Netanyahu, 47 per Eisenkot e 19 ai Partiti arabi

Commissione elettorale, al 50% dello spoglio delle schede: “Blocco Netanyahu in vantaggio”

Trump: “Dopo il mio endorsement rimonta clamorosa di Netanyahu”

Commissione elettorale: scrutinio al 25% assegna 63 seggi al blocco di Netanyahu

Netanyahu: “Opportunità storica e irripetibile per sconfiggere l’Iran una volta per tute”

Netanyahu: “Dobbiamo formare un governo nazionale forte di destra”

Leader della lista araba contattato da entrambi i blocchi politici, pro e contro Netanyahu

Il presidente israeliano Herzog: “Fare di tutto per evitare nuove elezioni”

"Dobbiamo fare di tutto, tanto più dopo la giornata di ieri, per evitare di dover ricorrere a ulteriori elezioni. Mi aspetto che chiunque arrivi qui" per le consultazioni post-voto "lo faccia con una mente aperta". E' il commento del presidente israeliano Isaac Herzog , alla luce della tornata elettorale che si è tenuta ieri nel Paese. Nessuno dei due blocchi principali ha la maggioranza mentre i partiti arabo-israeliani hanno registrato un exploit.

Scrutinio delle urne terminato: 53 seggi al blocco Netanyahu, 48 a blocco Eisenkot

Con il 100% dei voti delle urne scrutinati, 53 seggi vanno al blocco Netanyahu, 48 a quello del Cambiamento guidato da Eisenkot mentre 19 ai partiti arabi. Il voto ai seggi rappresenta l'86% del totale e ora mancano circa 650mila 'buste doppie' ancora da scrutinare che possono cambiare il quadro.

Netanyahu: “Non permetteremo una coalizione con i partiti arabi”

"Osama Saadi della 'Lista Unita' e alleato del blocco di sinistra dedica i risultati elettorali ai palestinesi a Gaza, in Giudea e Samaria e nella 'Gerusalemme occupata' ed elogia il popolo palestinese e i terroristi che si trovano in prigione. È con questi individui che intendono formare un governo pericoloso. Non permetteremo che ciò accada". Lo ha scritto Benjamin Netanyahu diffondendo un video del discorso ieri sera al quartier generale della 'Lista Unita' di Osama Saadi, ex parlamentare e candidato nella lista.

אוסאמה סעדי, השותף של גוש השמאל מהרשימה המשותפת, מקדיש את תוצאות הבחירות לפלסטינים בעזה, ביהודה ושומרון וב״ירושלים הכבושה״. הוא מהלל את העם הפלסטינים ואת המחבלים בכלא. עם אלה הם רוצים להקים ממשלה מסוכנת. לא ניתן לזה לקרות! https://t.co/ddwvdmTh7d

Media: il blocco di Eisenkot vuole nominare il nuovo presidente della Knesset con i voti dei partiti arabi

Il blocco di partiti di opposizione israeliani guidato da Gadi Eisenkot intende sfruttare i propri voti, insieme a quelli dei partiti arabi, per nominare un nuovo presidente della Knesset, incarico attualmente ricoperto da Amir Ohana, esponente del Likud. A riferirne è l'emittente israeliana Canale 12, mentre prosegue lo spoglio delle schede elettorali e regna ancora l'incertezza sulla formazione di un nuovo governo. Secondo quanto riportato, non sarebbe stato ancora individuato un candidato condiviso, sebbene siano stati fatti i nomi di Oded Forer, deputato di Yisrael Beytenu, ed Elazar Stern, della lista Yashar, come possibili opzioni. A riferirne è il Times of Israel .

Il Likud mantiene il controllo delle città al confine con il Libano e colpite da Hamas

Molte delle città e delle comunità israeliane più colpite dall'attacco di Hamas il 7 ottobre 2023 e dai missili lanciati da Hezbollah dal vicino Libano hanno confermato il loro sostegno al Likud del premier Benjamin Netanyahu. E' quanto emerge dall'analisi del voto secondo i risultati parziali. Kiryat Shmona, Shlomi, Avivim e Dovev, tutte situate lungo il confine settentrionale di Israele con il Libano, sono tra le comunità che hanno assegnato la percentuale maggiore dei loro voti al Likud. La maggior parte degli abitanti delle città di confine nel nord di Israele è stata evacuata per lunghi periodi a causa dei combattimenti delle Forze di difesa israeliane (Idf) contro il gruppo libanese di Hezbollah. Durante la guerra, Netanyahu ha avuto un lungo diverbio con il sindaco di Kiryat Shmona, Avichai Stern, membro del Likud, e si è recato raramente in città, nonostante fosse tra le più colpite dall'evacuazione di massa. Kiryat Shmona ha subito ingenti danni a causa dei razzi e dei droni lanciati da Hezbollah dal Libano, ma nonostante questo dallo spoglio aggiornato alle 12.30 emerge che circa il 48% dei voti in città è andato al Likud. Nel sud di Israele, il 39% degli elettori di Sderot ha votato per il Likud. Qui il 7 ottobre 2023 ben 53 persone sono state uccise durante l'assalto di Hamas.

Tajani: “Mi auguro che chi andrà al governo in Israele lavori per la pace”

Sulle elezioni politiche in Israele "vediamo i risultati finali. Io mi auguro che chiunque vada al governo lavori per la pace, per concludere questa stagione, che si trovi un accordo su Hormuz, che si trovi un accordo anche per garantire definitivamente la sicurezza di Israele, per dar vita a uno Stato palestinese che viva in pace con Israele, che riconosca Israele e sia riconosciuto da Israele". Lo ha detto il vicepremier e ministro degli Esteri, Antonio Tajani , all'assemblea di Confindustria Energia a Roma.

Scrutinio all’84,5%: 54 seggi al blocco Netanyahu, 49 seggi a quello Eisenkot, di Yashar, 17 ai partiti arabi

Con l'84,5% delle schede scrutinate, i risultati parziali pubblicati dalla Commissione elettorale centrale assegnano 54 seggi allo schieramento guidato dal primo ministro Benjamin Netanyahu e 49 seggi a quello guidato da Gadi Eisenkot, di Yashar. I partiti a guida araba - la Lista Comune e Ràam - scendono a 17 seggi

Il capo della Lista Unita araba: “Chi vuole un’alternativa a Netanyahu dovrà parlare con noi”

"Chiunque voglia offrire un'alternativa sostanziale e autentica al governo sanguinario di Netanyahu dovrà parlare con noi per spianare la strada al cambiamento che il popolo israeliano desidera ardentemente": lo ha dichiarato il presidente della Lista Unita (che riunisce tre partiti arabi) Yousef Jabareen, intendendo dire che qualsiasi partito aspiri a sostituire il governo di Benjamin Netanyahu dovrà dialogare con la sua fazione, dato che i risultati parziali delle elezioni mostrano che i partiti a guida araba potrebbero conquistare un numero senza precedenti di 19 seggi alla Knesset

Media: “Il conteggio definitivo dei voti delle doppie buste è atteso per venerdì”

Le schede elettorali delle elezioni legislative israeliane dovrebbero scrutinate nella giornata di oggi, ma non quelli delle cosiddette doppie buste, ossia i voti espressi per corrispondenza e a distanza, che potrebbero non essere completamente conteggiati fino a venerdì. La Commissione elettorale centrale stima che ci siano circa 600mila doppie buste, un aumento significativo rispetto alle elezioni del 2022. Considerando che ogni seggio alla Knesset equivale a circa 40mila voti, queste schede potrebbero avere un impatto significativo sul panorama politico finale. I voti contenuti in queste buste, la maggior parte dei quali proviene dai soldati delle Forze di Difesa Israeliane, tradizionalmente tendono a non favorire i partiti arabi e ultraortodossi (Haredi), osserva il Times of Israel. I voti dei soldati verranno conteggiati insieme alle altre schede pervenute tramite voto per corrispondenza, o in modalità equiparata, a partire da questa sera. Il sistema delle cosiddette "doppie buste" comprende anche i voti dei detenuti, del personale medico, delle persone affette da patologie e rappresentanti israeliani in missione all'estero

Il presidente statunitense Donald Trump ha detto di non aver ancora parlato con il primo ministro israeliano Benjamin Netanyahu, ma si è mostrato ottimista riguardo al risultato ottenuto dal leader del Likud mentre lo spoglio è ancora in corso. "Mi giungono voci che sia andato molto bene; la situazione è piuttosto combattuta", ha detto Trump parlando con i giornalisti presso la Joint Base Andrews, nel Maryland. "Potrebbe essere in vantaggio, o in una situazione di parità", ha detto. "E' ancora un pò presto, ma mi dicono che in Israele figure di primo piano commentano con stupore: "Wow", è andata molto meglio di quanto si pensasse". Il risultato finale potrebbe essere "una situazione di stallo o una vittoria, staremo a vedere", ha aggiunto Trump

items.title: China's families are now supporting more old people than kids
items.summary: The latest figures mark a major milestone as Beijing grapples with an ageing population.
items.content:
Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said.

Official data released in the last week , external show the ratio of China's dependent elderly people compared to the working age population rose to 23% last year, overtaking the figure for children, which stood at 22%.

The numbers are closely watched for signs of how China's shrinking workforce will impact both the world's second largest economy and global growth as a whole.

The latest figures mark a significant milestone as China grapples with an ageing population that could have implications for families, pensions and healthcare spending, analysts say.

China has been preparing for a growing proportion of elderly people in recent years, while urging younger generations to get married and for couples to have more children .

The latest data from China's National Bureau of Statistics show there are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above, accounting for nearly 16% of the country's total population.

At the same time there are about 213 million children aged 14 and under.

No official commentary was published with the statistics. But Chinese state-controlled news outlet Global Times wrote that the nation's "entry into a moderately ageing society" is the result of a mix of factors, including the "size of past birth cohorts" and longer life expectancy.

The shift could place added strain on pension, healthcare and long-term care systems, while also creating opportunities in the so-called silver economy that caters to older consumers, the newspaper said.

"It reflects a historical trend in demographic development rather than a short-term phenomenon," Global Times quoted one researcher as saying.

The demographic shift is "symbolic" and could suggest more public spending will move from families and schools to pensions and healthcare, said Professor Stuart Gietel-Basten from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

It may also pose a challenge to the country's ambitions, as it could limit its economic growth as well as people's spending power, said National University of Singapore sociology lecturer Mu Zheng.

China's ageing population has been driven by a mix of factors, including rapid urbanisation and the effects of the controversial one-child policy , which was in place from 1980 to the end of 2015.

The strategy, designed to keep China's rapid population growth under control, is estimated by the country's government to have prevented about 400 million births since it began, though this number has been contested.

The policy played a key role in shrinking the population and means there are fewer younger people to support a growing number of elderly relatives, Mu said.

But despite easing restrictions on the size of families, Beijing has struggled to persuade couples to have more children, with birth rates hitting historic lows.

Other contributing factors include changing gender roles, rising living costs and higher education levels that have put pressure on fertility rates, Mu said.

Beijing made further support for older people a part of the measures in its five-year economic blueprint that was announced earlier this year.

Financial help for pensioners has been a growing part of Chinese government spending. More than 53 million elderly people were receiving senior citizen allowances and subsidies by the end of 2025, according to official figures.

The Global Times noted that many people entering old age who were born between the 1950s and the 1970s have generally higher incomes compared to previous generations, stronger purchasing power and are healthier.

The dependency ratio is widely-used to measure ageing populations but it has also been questioned by some experts who argue that its scope is too limited.

Gietel-Basten said the use of the statistics risks "taking agency away" from older people - many of whom he says have been misrepresented as dependants.

It also does not take into account improvements to healthcare, he added.

items.title: Il giorno di Repubblica Insieme: oggi la Torino della cultura e del turismo disegna il suo futuro
items.summary: Il percorso per i 50 anni del quotidiano fa tappa a Camera: partecipano tra gli altri il direttore Cappellini, il costituzionalista Zagrebelsky, il sindaco Lo Russo. Appuntamento alle 17
items.content:
Turismo e cultura possono essere un motore di sviluppo per Torino , generare lavoro, attrarre investimenti e dare nuova vita ai suoi luoghi. La sfida è accompagnarne la crescita con un equilibrio che porti benefici anche a chi abita la città: nei servizi, nella qualità degli spazi pubblici, nelle opportunità di partecipazione.

Come si diventa una destinazione sempre più desiderata facendo crescere, insieme, la qualità della vita dei residenti? È la domanda al cuore di “Torino e l’arte di accogliere” , tappa torinese del viaggio di Repubblica Insieme nel cinquantenario del giornale fondato da Eugenio Scalfari.

Appuntamento oggi alle 17 a Camera – Centro Italiano per la Fotografia , in via delle Rosine 18 a Torino: il tema è «Turismo e cultura per una città aperta al mondo». In discussione c’è l’identità della città e il modo in cui viene raccontata, ma anche i collegamenti, l’ospitalità e la possibilità di costruire un’esperienza che inviti a tornare. Si analizzerà il rapporto tra luoghi della cultura e territorio, tra investimenti e servizi, tra la forza di un appuntamento capace di richiamare pubblico e la continuità di un’offerta che dura tutto l’anno.

L’apertura di Repubblica Insieme è affidata ai saluti della vicedirettrice di Repubblica Stefania Aloia e di Beniamino Pagliaro , caporedattore della redazione di Torino. Poi spazio all’intervento in collegamento da Roma del direttore Stefano Cappellini , seguito dal presidente emerito della Corte costituzionale e professore di Diritto costituzionale all’Università di Torino Gustavo Zagrebelsky . Un’occasione per approfondire il ruolo della stampa nella società contemporanea, tra responsabilità pubblica, pluralismo e qualità del dibattito democratico.

Il confronto si sposterà poi direttamente sui temi più rilevanti per la città con un’intervista a tutto campo al sindaco Stefano Lo Russo , condotta da Aloia e Pagliaro. A parlare specificamente di turismo, invece, ci saranno Andrea Andorno , amministratore delegato di Sagat, la società che gestisce l’aeroporto di Torino, e Matteo Sarzana , country manager Italia e Sud Europa di Airbnb. I due discuteranno di collegamenti, ospitalità e nuove opportunità per rendere la destinazione sempre più accessibile e competitiva. A moderare sarà il giornalista Stefano Parola .

Toccherà quindi alla giornalista Ottavia Giustetti coordinare l’incontro “Fare cultura, fare territorio” che vedrà a confronto Roberta Ceretto di Cantine Ceretto e Maurizia Rebola , direttrice editoriale e culturale di “Vale” Polo Culturale. Al termine si terrà la proiezione di un estratto dal docufilm di Ezio Mauro “Repubblica 50” , dedicato alla storia del quotidiano.

L’ingresso all’appuntamento di Repubblica è gratuito con registrazione online all’indirizzo web larep.it/torino28 , oppure tramite il QR code in questa pagina. Si potrà anche visitare la mostra di Letizia Battaglia da poco inaugurata a Camera.

items.title: Manovra e mancette elettorali: “le termiti” che erodono il bilancio dello Stato
items.summary: Outlook del 28 ottobre. Iscriviti alla Newsletter
items.content:
Benvenuti su Outlook, la newsletter di Repubblica che analizza l'economia, la finanza, i mercati internazionali. Ogni mercoledì parleremo di società quotate e no, di personaggi, istituzioni, di scandali e inchieste legate a questo mondo. Se volete scrivermi, la mia mail è w.galbiati@repubblica.it.

Le “termiti” continuano a erodere il bilancio dello Stato. E lo fanno dal suo interno. Così vengono chiamate le tax expenditures dagli economisti che ogni anno, da dieci a questa parte, compilano l’elenco di quelle eccezioni al pagamento delle tasse che fanno dell’Italia un campione mondiale.

Il documento . Il Rapporto annuale sulle spese fiscali ha calcolato che il buco dei mancati versamenti o abbuoni per il 2026 sarà di 129,7 miliardi di euro , in crescita rispetto ai 118,9 miliardi dell’anno precedente. Un importo pari a sei manovre fiscali messe insieme.

La manovra pre-elettorale . L’ammanco fa ancora più impressione nei giorni in cui il ministro dell’Economia, Giancarlo Giorgetti , si affanna a cercare le coperture per una manovra che dovrebbe aggirarsi intorno ai 23 miliardi di euro .

E in cui tutti i partiti di maggioranza non fanno altro che aggiungere deroghe su deroghe nelle loro proposte per quella che sarà l’ ultima legge di bilancio prima delle elezioni .

Più volte il ministro dell’Economia ha ribadito la volontà di razionalizzare le tax expenditures, ma non è mai andato oltre le parole .

Le nuove proposte . Il suo partito, la Lega , propone addirittura di incrementarle. In particolare, Matteo Salvini ripete come un disco rotto che le agevolazioni fiscali per le partite Iva debbano salire da 85mila a 100 mila euro .

Il regime forfettario consente alle persone fisiche, in genere professionisti, di non addebitare l’Iva ai propri clienti e di pagare solo il 15% di tasse , senza rispettare i normali scaglioni Irpef.

Inizialmente l’aliquota era applicabile per chi aveva un giro di affari fino 65mila euro , poi alzato nel 2022 a 85mila euro , un limite che si vorrebbe portare, se non in questa in una delle prossime manovre, a 100mila euro .

Con i vecchi limiti, questo giochetto, secondo i numeri contenuti nel Rapporto annuale sulle spese fiscali , costa all’Erario ben 3,5 miliardi di euro l’anno di mancate tasse .

Forza Italia non è da meno . Oltre a una no tax area per gli under 30 , il partito di Tajani insiste sul taglio dell'Irpef per il ceto medio, estendendo l' aliquota del 33% alla fascia di reddito tra 50mila e i 60mila euro (invece dell'attuale 43%).

Il costo stimato per lo Stato sarebbe tra i 2,7 e i 3 miliardi di euro l'anno .

Fratelli d’Italia . Ma il record di nuove tax expenditures spetta al partito della premier. La prima è estendere la cedolare secca al 21% agli affitti di immobili commerciali , da abbassare al 10% nei centri metropolitani .

Oggi questa agevolazione per le normali abitazioni crea già un buco da 3,3 miliardi l’anno , destinato ovviamente a crescere se estesa anche ai negozi.

Sul fronte del lavoro , Fratelli d’Italia propone di aumentare la deduzione dalle tasse che le imprese possono attuare quando assumono i giovani lavoratori sotto i 30 anni o categorie da proteggere come le donne con figli o i disabili.

Attualmente le imprese possono detrarre fino al 130% del costo del dipendente , una concessione che costa allo Stato 1,3 miliardi di euro .

La premier suggerisce di portare questa deduzione al 130-140% di base e di alzarla fino al 180% per le madri lavoratrici .

Ma le proposte di Fratelli d’Italia non si fermano qui e vanno dalla flat tax al 5% sui redditi dei neoassunti under 35 alla tassazione sempre al 5% degli aumenti salariali dovuti ai rinnovi contrattuali fino alla detassazione delle tredicesime .

Per non parlare poi della cancellazione del bollo auto fino a 80kw che toglie allo Stato 2,3 miliardi sui 7,5 miliardi di gettito garantito dalla tassazione delle auto.

Non tutto il male vien per nuocere . Premesso che alcune proposte possono essere auspicabili e condivisibili , la saga delle tax expenditures è tuttavia lungi dal ridimensionarsi e dal perdere quella connotazione elettorale che la contraddistingue.

Prima di introdurne di nuove, o almeno contestualmente, andrebbe rivisto l’intero sistema per creare quella razionalizzazione di spesa che oggi manca, dandogli magari anche un senso distributivo .

Il trend . Dal 2022 ad oggi , invece, sebbene le agevolazioni siano numericamente scese, il conto per lo Stato non ha fatto altro che aumentare e questa manovra che il governo si appresta ad approvare non è da meno.

Limitandosi alle misure erariali, senza dunque le agevolazioni fiscali locali, quando si è insediato il governo Meloni erano in vigore 626 tax expenditures contro le 573 attuali .

Eppure, il minor gettito per le casse dello Stato è cresciuto da 82,6 a 118,9 miliardi , con la prospettiva di salire ulteriormente nell’anno in corso a 129,7 miliardi di euro .

Le spese più conosciute . Nella categoria delle spese fiscali rientrano molte voci che chi compila il 730 conosce alla perfezione. Si va dagli sconti per le spese sanitarie , agli interessi sul mutuo , da quelle per gli animali domestici alle tasse per la scuola dei figli fino ai funerali .

Quelle meno conosciute . Ma ve ne sono molte altre di cui non si immagina nemmeno l’esistenza e sono talmente tante e mirate che gli esperti del Mef non esitano a chiamarle dei v eri e propri favori elettorali che riguardano ogni settore, dall’ agricoltura ai trasporti , dalle imprese alle banche , dalla casa alle persone fisiche fino alle varie associazioni no profit.

Il primato italiano . L’Italia ha un primato nelle tax expenditures , non tanto in percentuale sul Pil, quanto in numero di voci , che sono parecchie , con un importo basso , se non a volte trascurabile, e con pochi e mirati beneficiari .

Ben 139 misure fiscali hanno un costo in termini di gettito inferiore ai 10 milioni e altre 143 sono definite trascurabili . Insieme valgono poco, ma tradiscono la loro natura clientelare .

Poche ma pesanti . Sono invece 23 le voci che hanno un peso superiore al miliardo di euro , rappresentano solo il 4% delle tax expenditures , ma impattano complessivamente per 108 miliardi sui conti del Tesoro.

La classifica . Dividendo le agevolazioni in base alle Missioni del bilancio dello Stato e calcolando gli effetti finanziari in termini di mancato gettito , per il 2026 risulta che la Missione con un costo maggiore è la numero 19, “ Casa e assetto urbanistico ” con circa 71,7 miliardi di euro , seguita dalla Missione 26, “ Politiche per il lavoro ” con un passivo di 17,3 miliardi di euro e dalla Missione 11, “ Competitività e sviluppo delle imprese ” con circa 12,3 miliardi di euro .

Seguono le Missioni 24, “ Diritti sociali, politiche sociali e famiglia ” con circa 7,6 miliardi di euro , la Missione 20, “ Tutela della salute ” con circa 6,5 miliardi di euro e la Missione 29 “ Politiche economico- finanziarie e di bilancio e tutela della finanza pubblica ” con circa 3,2 miliardi di euro .

Il settore più agevolato . Il primato negativo spetta dunque alla Casa , dove, oltre alla cedolare secca (3,3 miliardi) e agli interessi sui mutui per la prima casa (1,3 miliardi), incidono soprattutto i vari bonus edilizi che sono stati rinnovati, e solo in parte ridotti, dai governi che si sono succeduti.

Per il 2026 , l’ Ecobonus pesa per 15,2 miliardi , il Superbonus per 16,9 miliardi , le ristrutturazioni per 10,8 miliardi , il Sisma bonus per 10,1 miliardi , il bonus facciate per 2,8 miliardi , una valanga di soldi che dovrebbe far riflettere prima di introdurre una qualsiasi nuova tax expenditures .

La proiezione . Nei prossimi due anni, basterebbe stare fermi . Se non venissero rinnovati gli sconti nelle manovre 2027 e 2028, il buco nei conti dello Stato dovuto ai bonus edilizi dovrebbe passare dai 53,1 miliardi del 2026 ai 15,1 miliardi del 2028 .

Political economy . Porre un freno alle tax expenditures, razionalizzandole, è un obiettivo che dovrebbero avere tutti i governi, perché oggi la “ political economy” delle spese fiscali ha poco a che fare con obiettivi tributari , distributivi o di efficienza .

Sono per lo più, secondo gli stessi esperti del Mef, “ un sussidio tributario – che equivale a una spesa diretta – che emerge nel processo di scambio con i gruppi di pressione ”. Insomma mancette elettorali .

Il danno . “Le tax expenditures sono vere e proprie termiti che possono lentamente logorare la struttura dei sistemi tributari ”, ha scritto più volte il gruppo di lavoro guidato dal professore Mauro Marè .

“Se non si interviene con misure adeguate, le termiti indeboliscono il funzionamento di qualsiasi sistema tributario, lasciando come opzione ai vari governi solo quella di aggiungere ai regimi promossi dal governo precedente, altri regimi di favore per le varie constituencies . Le spese fiscali creano un’ elevata dipendenza da cui è complicato liberarsi”.

Per uscirne serve un’azione mirata e organica che, con un debito al 138% del Pil , non possiamo più rinviare .

items.title: Ceasefire extended across Ukraine's Kherson region, officials say
items.summary: The truce was originally planned for the stranded residents of Oleshky, and Russia and Ukraine say no breaches have been reported.
items.content:
A ceasefire that began with the aim of getting food and medicine to the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been extended across the wider southern region of Kherson, according to sources.

Several thousand residents are trapped in the city with no access to food, water and electricity. On one side is the Dnipro river, while Russian forces are on the other and all the roads out are too dangerous.

However, no breaches of the truce that began early on Tuesday have so far been reported.

US First Lady Melania Trump, who helped broker the ceasefire along with Pope Leo XIV, said on Tuesday that the area involved had been expanded to provide "safe passage" for humanitarian convoys.

That was later corroborated by the press secretary to Ukraine's public ombudsman, and by Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of Kherson, who said Russian shelling had stopped both in Kherson city, which is in Ukrainian hands, and the wider region.

Under the deal, the ceasefire will be followed by deliveries of humanitarian aid to Oleshky and then evacuations, planned for Friday, for anyone wishing to leave.

An estimated 1,700 to 2,000 people remain in Oleshky itself and a few thousand more in surrounding areas.

Many residents have resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive, telling the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger and want to leave.

Both sides said the ceasefire was being observed. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said everything was proceeding "according to plan", and paid tribute to US mediation and in particular representatives of Melania Trump.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said if the ceasefire produced results, it could "pave the way for other steps in the peace process".

A key official in President Volodymyr Zelensky's parliamentary party, David Arakhamia, said it would continue until 22:59 Ukrainian time on Sunday 1 November, and described the truce as the "largest de-escalation since 2022".

Before the war Oleshky was home to 24,000 people, but it was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

No shops are open, and the city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka Dam was blown up in 2023, flooding the area and killing many people in Oleshky itself.

Conditions have become so desperate that not only is getting supplies into the city extremely difficult, but escaping is too risky because the routes out of Oleshky have been mined and subject to drone attack.

One woman told the BBC she had stepped on a landmine and was currently in hospital where she had undergone two operations: "I don't know how long I will have to spend there," she said, worried about not being able to join the evacuation.

Pope Leo appealed earlier this month to Russia's President Vladimir Putin to allow food and medical aid into Oleshky as well as a safe evacuation, and urged his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky to co-operate with Moscow over a ceasefire.

Then the White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire.

On Tuesday, the US first lady said on X that the area covered by the ceasefire "has expanded beyond Oleshky, within the Kherson region, to provide safe passage for the humanitarian convoys".

The current truce is supposed to enable roads to be cleared of mines for supplies to get into the city possibly on Thursday, and for residents to have safe passage out in an evacuation planned for Friday.

Russia's defence ministry said units from the army's Dnepr group had been conducting "engineering reconnaissance" and clearing main access roads into the village of "explosive and booby-trap devices".

Many details on the evacuation plans are unclear, and residents are wary of trusting officials with their names and addresses. However, a local volunteer told the BBC that about 500 people had already expressed interest by Tuesday afternoon.

Vladimir Saldo, the Russian-installed head of occupied areas of Kherson, said temporary accommodation had been prepared in the region itself as well as Russian-annexed Crimea and across the Russian border in the Rostov, Krasnodar and Stavropol regions.

Saldo told Russian media that most Oleshky residents wanted to leave the city and stay in Russia, although his account has not been corroborated on the ground.

It is hard to make contact with people there as communication is patchy and many are reluctant to speak of the situation in fear of reprisals from the Russians.

Those residents or relatives who have spoken to the BBC have expressed fears that Russia may not allow them to return to Ukraine, or might examine their phones and online activity for signs of Ukrainian support, which could put them in danger.

Ukraine's military general staff urged people not to trust unverified reports or spread rumours about "the routes, time and place of the movement of people and humanitarian convoys".

White House says Melania Trump brokered truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster'

Eating garden weeds to survive in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water

To stay or risk the 'Road of Death' - Ukrainian civilians trapped in frontline city

Zelensky has warned that routes out of Oleshky that are demined by Russia will ensure that those civilians leaving Oleshky will "head towards Russia and stay there".

He said some residents would get to Ukrainian-controlled territory "one way or another", and that ideally anyone trapped would be able to reach their destination and evacuate to Ukraine.

One resident called Serhii, who fled Oleshky through minefields around three weeks ago, said he had eventually returned to Ukraine via Russia and Belarus. He called for a route across the River Dnipro that avoided Russian-occupied territory, saying "you simply cannot trust the Russian Federation".

However, bridges across the River Dnipro have been destroyed and sources say the riverbank is also mined and dangerous, so crossing into Ukrainian-controlled territory appears impossible.

Across the river, in Kherson city, no explosions have been heard and no drone-related injuries reported since 03:00 (01:00 GMT) on Tuesday and cars and pedestrians have been moving freely, according to local reports.

"Judging from the fact that more people are walking around, it feels a bit calmer," Galina Kyrychenko, a resident in the city, told public broadcaster Suspilne.

items.title: Alle elezioni in Israele l’affluenza è stata la più alta da quasi trent’anni
items.summary: Ha votato il 77,7 per cento degli aventi diritto, tra cui moltissimi arabi e persone tornate apposta dall'estero
items.content:
Alle elezioni israeliane del 27 ottobre ha votato il 77,7 per cento degli aventi diritto; è stata l’affluenza più alta dal 1999, quando raggiunse il 78,7 per cento.

La partecipazione è stata tanta anche tra le persone arabe israeliane, che votano storicamente meno della media nazionale per sfiducia, boicottaggio volontario o perché non sono rappresentate dai partiti.

Negli ultimi anni gli abusi contro di loro sono diventati sempre più frequenti, così come sono sempre più gravi i problemi nelle loro comunità, a partire dalla criminalità organizzata, anche a causa dell’indifferenza delle autorità israeliane.

In base ai primi exit poll i partiti arabi potrebbero aver ottenuto 16 o 17 seggi, il numero più alto di sempre (non avevano mai superato i 15). In questo caso potrebbero rivelarsi cruciali nelle trattative per formare un governo, necessarie perché nessuna coalizione ha ottenuto la maggioranza.

Per votare sono tornati in Israele anche decine di migliaia di persone israeliane che vivono all’estero (non c’è la possibilità di votare da fuori), segno che queste elezioni erano percepite come particolarmente importanti anche dagli israeliani che vivono all’estero.

Queste elezioni sono state le prime dagli attacchi di Hamas in Israele del 7 ottobre 2023, e quindi le prime dall’inizio della guerra nella Striscia di Gaza e delle successive operazioni militari di Israele in Medio Oriente . Tutti i principali leader politici avevano presentato le elezioni come decisive per il futuro di Israele, e durante la campagna elettorale, fino a martedì stesso, hanno fatto continui appelli per invitare le persone ad andare a votare.

items.title: La Corte d’Appello ha confermato la decadenza del presidente della Valle d’Aosta, Renzo Testolin
items.content:
La Corte d’Appello di Torino ha confermato la decadenza del presidente della Valle d’Aosta, Renzo Testolin, ordinata dal tribunale a maggio per aver superato il limite di tre mandati consecutivi previsto dalla legge della regione. La sentenza è già in vigore ma Testolin può comunque fare ricorso alla Corte di Cassazione. La sua giunta quindi è decaduta e da domani nel consiglio regionale dovrebbero cominciare le consultazioni per formare un nuovo esecutivo.

Testolin, del partito autonomista Union Valdôtaine, aveva fatto parte della giunta regionale come assessore e poi come presidente in tre legislature regionali (quelle iniziate nel 2013, 2018, 2020) e a novembre 2025 era stato infine riconfermato alla presidenza della regione, dopo che era risultato il candidato più votato alle elezioni regionali di settembre. L’attuale mandato di Testolin è quindi il quarto consecutivo nella giunta.

In Valle d’Aosta il presidente non viene eletto direttamente, a differenza delle altre regioni: si vota la composizione del consiglio regionale secondo un sistema proporzionale puro, poi i 35 membri eletti eleggono il presidente. Anche per questo la decadenza del presidente non comporta automaticamente nuove elezioni.

items.title: Trump says US voter fraud is 'rampant' - evidence suggests it is extremely rare
items.summary: As the US president casts doubt on the security of the midterm elections, BBC Verify examines his claims.
items.content:
President Donald Trump has offered a $1m (£750,000) reward to people who report cases of voter fraud in the US which lead to a conviction.

Ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, Trump has been casting doubt on the security of the vote - alleging "rampant" cheating in postal voting and non-citizens voting.

However, studies suggest actual cases of these are extremely rare.

BBC Verify has taken a look at the evidence and Trump's proposed changes to the voting system.

For years, Trump has made repeated unsubstantiated claims that postal voting leads to widespread fraud.

He has also encouraged Republicans to vote by mail in the midterms and has said he has cast his ballot by post in the past.

The president has been unsuccessful in his push for Congress to pass an act which would only allow people to vote by mail if they are disabled, ill, serving in the military, or travelling.

The majority of states allow , external people to vote by mail without having to provide a reason, and in the 2024 presidential election about 48 million people cast postal ballots.

Trump signed an executive order last year which directed the US Postal Service to only deliver ballots to voters on lists of citizens compiled by government agencies. It also sought to require states to use the same envelope style for postal votes.

Trump criticises Supreme Court after justices block mail-in ballot restrictions

However, the order was rejected by the US Supreme Court which called such changes so close to the midterm elections "arbitrary and capricious" - but said it could revisit the issue afterwards.

US states have different rules for verifying postal ballots, but every state matches certain voter information on the ballots against what they have on file to check they are eligible and most also conduct signature checks , external .

Studies of multiple US elections suggest postal vote fraud has been extremely rare.

The Brookings Institution policy research think tank , external looked at the 2016, 2018, 2020 and 2022 elections and found an average of about four cases of fraud out of every 10 million postal votes.

The report used a database kept by the Heritage Foundation - a think tank which has been aligned with Trump in the past - which records cases of electoral fraud that have ended in a conviction.

We looked back in the database , external over the last 20 years and found it has tallied 325 convictions as a result of the fraudulent use of postal ballots.

A 2020 study by the American Statistical Association , external looked at cases of voter fraud in eight states which send postal ballots to all eligible voters and found no evidence that voting by mail increased the risk of voter fraud overall.

For example, according to the study, Oregon recorded 40 fraud cases between 2000 and 2020 having sent out more than 100 million postal ballots over that period.

Trump has claimed non-citizen voting is widespread, and prior to the 2024 election he said Democrats were allowing millions of migrants into the US "so they can vote, vote, vote".

It is illegal for non-citizens to vote in US federal elections - punishments can include a prison sentence, a fine, and deportation.

The voting act the president has pushed Congress to pass would require voters to show a government-issued photo identification before they cast their ballots, as well as proof of citizenship when registering to vote and ongoing citizenship verification.

Critics have raised concerns that stricter voter ID requirements could harm voter turnout as people may not have a passport or the required government-issued photo ID.

"We don't have a national ID card that the government gives out, unlike a lot of countries. Drivers licence is most common but it doesn't identify your immigration status so the ID that most Americans carry around wouldn't be enough for you to vote," says Jonathan Diaz, a voting rights expert at the Campaign Legal Center.

A 2023 survey by the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice , external suggested that about 21.3 million voting-age American citizens, or about 9%, do not have documents proving citizenship readily available.

However, others argue that there has been no noticeable impact from existing voter ID laws.

"When scholars look at the effect of voter ID laws - either what the conservatives say on fraud or what progressive groups warn against about voter suppression - there doesn't seem to be a lot of proof that either has happened," says Walter Olson, an election expert at the conservative Cato Institute.

A number of largely Republican-run states have tightened voter ID requirements in the last couple of years. There have been 21 restrictive voting laws enacted since the 2024 election to establish stricter ID requirements, according to a study by the Brennan Center for Justice , external .

Multiple studies show proven instances of non-citizens voting in past US elections have been very small.

The Heritage Foundation's database identified 24 cases of non-citizens being convicted for voting between 2005 and 2025.

A 2026 analysis by Reuters , external of non-citizen voting cases brought in federal courts found that over the last 30 years 129 people have been criminally charged and 73 of those cases resulted in a conviction.

"The fact that it's illegal for non-citizens to vote is a pretty strong deterrent in the first place as many worry about their immigration status and it would be an extremely risky move to vote," says Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution.

"There's never been any evidence that there are many people who have done that, certainly not enough to influence an election."

Trump has also pushed for states to use a federal database - the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (Save) database - to identify voters suspected of being non-citizens and remove them from voter rolls.

The tool has access to information about naturalised citizens and non-citizens who have contacted the federal government previously. It was launched in the 1980s to help government agencies verify individuals' eligibility for government benefits based on their immigration status.

Critics have questioned the reliability of using the data to remove people from voter rolls as they say it could be outdated and include people who have since become US citizens - but the US Supreme Court has lifted restrictions on the Trump administration using it this way.

US Supreme Court allows Trump to use controversial database to check voter citizenship

"Federal databases can be invaluable to states trying to update their voter rolls so long as their limitations are understood," says Olson. "So part of the Trump plan which requires the sharing of information is positive, even if the second part to require states to treat the database contents as reliable despite their continuing evident gaps and inaccuracies is bad."

The use of the programme by individual states is voluntary, and from those who have used it recently the number of non-citizens detected has been small.

In Georgia, after an audit of the state's voter rolls, 432 possible non-citizens were identified , external on its voter rolls over 30 years.

The Department of Homeland Security provided Nevada with a list of 185 names which it claimed identified non-citizens who had been improperly allowed to register to vote, but state officials found that they were all in fact citizens. , external

The White House has pointed to a case in New Jersey, where this summer a software glitch in the state's drivers licensing department registered about 6,600 non-citizens to vote between June 2023 and June 2024. State officials have said fewer than 400 cast ballots and they have all now been removed from the system.

The US Justice Department requested that California doesn't count 20,000 postal ballots ahead of the midterms from people it claims are "likely non-citizen registrants" - but that request has been rejected by an appeals court.

Out of that 20,000, it has charged 28 people , external who the department says are non-citizens who had illegally registered to vote.

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here . Those outside the UK can sign up here .

items.title: Ex-wife of Zimbabwe's vice-president freed after collapse of attempted murder case
items.summary: Marry Mubaiwa had been held on remand for seven years after being charged in 2019 for her then husband's attempted murder.
items.content:
The former wife of Zimbabwe's vice-president has been freed from remand after seven years while on trial for his attempted murder.

Marry Mubaiwa was charged in 2019, after her then husband Gen Constantino Chiwenga accused her of trying to impede his medical treatment in South Africa.

Ordering her release, a magistrate said Mubaiwa had suffered mental, physical and financial prejudice during the trial, state-owned daily the Herald said.

The ruling was made after the state asked for the trial to be postponed by a month in order to engage witnesses.

Her lawyer described the ruling as a victory that had come too late, because her client's rights had been violated by the delay in the trial.

Speaking outside court in the capital Harare on Tuesday, the lawyer added that if the state moved for a new trial, they would deal with it when it happened.

Mubaiwa was accused of attempting to kill Chiwenga, while he was in hospital in Pretoria. The vice-president then went to China for four months of treatment.

According to the New Zimbabwe news website, Mubaiwa celebrated her release outside court, and said justice had been achieved and that she was proud of her lawyer.

In 2017, Chiwenga played a key role in overthrowing then President Robert Mugabe.

items.title: Il presidente finlandese e il primo ministro norvegese hanno fatto una rara telefonata a Putin
items.content:
Il presidente finlandese Alexander Stubb e il primo ministro norvegese Jonas Gahr Støre hanno telefonato al presidente russo Vladimir Putin, un raro contatto diretto fra leader europei e quello russo. La chiamata è durata un’ora e mezzo e ha riguardato la guerra in Ucraina: non ha portato a sviluppi concreti. I leader europei, che erano a Helsinki, hanno detto di aver parlato dei futuri colloqui di pace , previsti a novembre negli Emirati Arabi Uniti. Il governo russo ha detto che Putin ha riaffermato le proprie rivendicazioni massimaliste sull’Ucraina.

Finlandia e Norvegia hanno governi che hanno mantenuto una linea molto dura contro la Russia e di sostegno all’Ucraina. Il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky ha ringraziato Stubb e Støre per il sostegno dimostrato con la telefonata. Nelle ultime settimane la posizione dell’amministrazione di Donald Trump si è avvicinata più del solito a Putin , spingendo alcuni leader europei a cercare un ruolo maggiore nelle trattative sulla guerra in Ucraina, in cui hanno finora avuto un ruolo marginale. L’ultima telefonata del genere era stata fatta dal presidente francese Emmanuel Macron nel 2025.

La chiamata non era stata concordata con gli altri leader europei né con le istituzioni dell’Unione Europea (di cui la Norvegia non fa parte). Per questo la scelta ha ricevuto qualche critica, fra cui dal primo ministro svedese Ulf Kristersson, che ha auspicato maggiore coordinamento diplomatico fra i paesi europei, e dalla prima ministra danese Mette Friedriksen.

items.title: Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.anthropic.com/research/early-progress-drug-development Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50265609 Points: 259 # Comments: 254
items.content:
Anthropic’s life sciences team is working to accelerate curing disease. Over the past several months, our scientists have engaged in deep research partnerships with six organizations developing new medicines: BigHat Biosciences , Bristol Myers Squibb , Divergence Labs , Enveda , Generate Biomedicines , and The Column Group . We've also begun drug discovery efforts of our own. In doing so, we've learned a lot about how Claude can support drug development, and how we’ll need to improve Claude further to realize AI's potential in medicine. We plan to scale this work up substantially from here .

There are many opportunities to speed up drug development, even beyond the most commonly discussed applications of AI, like proposing initial designs for new molecules. Developing a drug involves many varied tasks: doing early research to identify a target for a drug and the right type of drug to engage it, designing a molecule with the right properties, optimizing it to be manufactured reliably at scale, drafting the regulatory filings needed to run clinical trials, designing and administering those trials, and much more.

Our strategy to realize AI’s medical benefits is based on having AI increasingly involved in all of these tasks. There is no single problem to solve; the bottlenecks are distributed all throughout the drug development process. The best way to identify and work through these bottlenecks is to get deeply involved in real drug programs, across many different disease areas and stages of development.

So, over the past several months, we’ve partnered with six organizations to do so. We’ve also started drug discovery efforts of our own, including programs for rare childhood forms of muscular dystrophy, where Claude handles much of the scientific and operational work.

This work serves our goals in three ways. First, it lets us better understand the strengths and limitations of our models in relation to a much wider range of drug development tasks (we’ve already prioritized specific improvements to our models based on what we’ve learned so far). Second, these programs can serve as case studies for the wider life sciences community. If Claude is to significantly increase the rate of new cures, we need to work with many more biotechnology firms and integrate Claude more deeply into their development processes. Third, these projects should, if their positive trajectories continue, have direct impact themselves. We’re optimistic that some may result in effective new medicines for the diseases they target, including food allergies, rare childhood diseases, and several forms of cancer.

In this post, we provide an update on our progress with our partners, along with technical reports and preprints that describe our thought process, methods, and early results in more detail. We then briefly outline where our work is headed next.

Generate Biomedicines: modality engineering. Generate Biomedicines has been working on increasing the usefulness of a cancer treatment known as CAR T-cell therapy. This therapy has historically helped treat blood cell cancers; Generate aims to reengineer it so that it can treat solid tumor cancers too. To do this, they’re aiming to shorten one part of the therapy’s genetic instructions, which would create room for additional instructions suited to other kinds of cancer. Six Generate scientists used Claude Code to propose new designs for this part. One design was about 70% shorter than the standard version, and in lab tests it was more effective: it allowed immune cells to make roughly 10 times as many receptors (the proteins they use to spot cancer cells), it killed tumor cells more efficiently, and the immune cells remained active for longer. Read more , and see Generate’s technical report .

Divergence Labs: hit generation. Divergence Labs is working on a novel way to treat food allergies. Food allergies are set off by a reaction from a molecule called IgE, some of which is attached to our immune cells and some of which floats freely in our blood. Divergence Labs is developing drugs that would detach the IgE from our immune cells entirely, rather than solely neutralizing the IgE circulating in our blood, as standard medications do. This could provide a much more effective treatment, but it requires a precise design, with two “arms”: one that would bind tightly to IgE, and another that would help prise IgE from the immune cell. Claude converted Divergence Labs’ goals into a detailed design plan, and then, largely autonomously, generated roughly 35,000 antibody designs in about a month to be narrowed down and tested. In those early tests, Divergence found “hits” for both arms: three designs that could bind to IgE, and 20 that could dislodge it. Three of those 20 appeared to dislodge IgE more than the standard medication. Its next step is to build a drug that combines the two arms. Read more , and see Divergence’s technical report .

BigHat Biosciences: lead optimization. BigHat Biosciences pairs AI with an automated lab to improve potential drugs (or “leads”), which must bind their target tightly, remain stable through manufacturing and storage, and avoid clumping together (among other criteria). BigHat’s scientists and an Anthropic researcher worked with Claude to improve these three properties in two leads, both antibody fragments that could become parts of future drugs: one designed to target cancer cells, and one designed to keep a drug in the body longer. Claude, connected to BigHat’s lab data system, Reccy, proposed changes to each molecule, and BigHat’s lab made and tested about 1,010 variants in about 10 weeks. Partway through, the team suspected the standard heat-stability and clumping metrics were misleading. Claude and the researcher reanalyzed the raw data, then proposed different metrics and a protocol change to test them. BigHat’s scientists refined and ran it, and the main predictions held. Compared with the originals, the best versions bound more than 10x more tightly, the cancer-targeting lead stayed in solution 18°C higher, and the lead for longer-lasting drugs clumped more than 100x more slowly. Read more , and see BigHat’s technical report .

Enveda: manufacturing and filings. To conduct clinical trials, companies need records showing that each batch of a new drug has been made to strict quality standards, and to submit an application to regulators, among other requirements. At Enveda, manufacturing chemists spent up to 75% of their time on paperwork. To ease the load, Enveda built a system that connects all of its manufacturing documents to Claude, then lets Claude flag any possible issues. Over tests on 1,061 pages of documentation, Claude caught all 11 issues that human reviewers had spotted—and flagged seven they’d missed. In the process, this method reduced human review time by 89%, from over 25 hours to less than three. Separately, Claude wrote the first drafts of two important regulatory documents. One took four hours, compared to about three months by hand. For the other, Enveda’s standard human review process found one minor error. Read more , and see Enveda’s technical report .

The Column Group (TCG): company creation. Because drug discovery can be slow, expensive, and prone to failure, investors in biotechnology companies have favored safer, previously validated ideas over riskier new ones, even when the latter could help more patients. We’ve been working with TCG to see whether Claude can change this by cutting the time and cost of drug discovery so that investors can confidently support more ambitious ideas. Specifically, TCG is establishing Pleiades, a new company that will use Claude to run many more—and more complex—drug programs than is usual for a small team. This could be a model for how Claude can reduce both the scientific and the operational and administrative overhead required to run a biotechnology company. If this works, this model could be replicated across the industry and direct investment toward harder problems in medicine. Pleiades is currently developing new tools and workflows for Claude; its very first Claude skill, which helps Claude assess whether drug targets are worth pursuing, has been evaluated on 45 target-disease pairs. Read more .

More recently, we’ve also begun working with Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) to find and address bottlenecks in clinical trial planning. BMS is using Claude to assess plans of an early-stage drug in clinical trials, and to estimate the likelihood of those trials succeeding. Together, we plan to expand this work in 2027 to understand its potential for increasing the probability of success in early development.

Michael Pourdehnad, MD , Senior Vice President, Head of Early Clinical Development, Hematology, Oncology and Cell Therapy.

In addition to our work with these partners, we’ve begun to run some research programs ourselves. We’ve acquired Mithril Medicine, a one-person company that has been developing treatments for two rare forms of muscular dystrophy. Its founder, Cody Tranbarger, used Claude to organize contracts, logistics, and experiments with 11 external labs, and delegated many other aspects of Mithril’s operations to Claude. As a result, Mithril took a possible treatment for one form of muscular dystrophy from an idea to promising results in mice in less than 18 months. Now at Anthropic, Cody is continuing this research, and plans to start several new programs. If his drug candidates continue to hold up, we expect a drug to be ready to start clinical trials in humans as soon as late 2028. Read more and see our technical report .

items.title: Raspberry Pi Zero 3W and Pi 4 Model A spotted in device trees
items.summary: Article URL: https://bret.dk/raspberry-pi-zero-3-w-pi-4-model-a/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50265594 Points: 186 # Comments: 108
items.content:
Two new Raspberry Pi boards have quietly turned up in Raspberry Pi’s Linux kernel tree, and neither of them is quite what I’d have guessed. Device tree files for a Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W and a Raspberry Pi 4 Model A have landed ( Phoronix also spotted it ), and whilst there’s no official announcement just yet, device tree files tend to give away a surprising amount if you can decipher them and I gave it my best shot.

The Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W launched almost exactly five years ago (tomorrow, in fact), so a successor has been a loooooong time coming. If you want a refresher on where things stood back then, my Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W vs Zero W benchmarks piece covers the jump from the original pretty well.

The headline from the Zero 3 W device tree is the SoC. It’s the Broadcom BCM2711 , the same quad-core Cortex-A72 chip that powers the Raspberry Pi 4 , replacing the Zero 2 W’s quad-core 1GHz Cortex-A53 RP3A0. If you want an idea of the sort of gap we’re talking about, it’s worth having a look at how those two compare on sbc.compare . That’s a big step up in per-core performance, and if they can get anything close to Pi 4 clocks in that tiny footprint, it’ll be a hell of a lot of compute for a Zero. I do wonder how toasty it’s going to get though, as the BCM2711 isn’t exactly known for running cool, and there’s not a lot of board for the heat to spread into. The device tree doesn’t tell us anything about clock speeds, so we’ll have to wait and see whether it’s been dialled back.

There are a couple of more speculative bits too. The PCIe controller is enabled and there are lines named PCIE_PWR_EN and PCIE_DET_WAKE, and the camera side pulls in a 4-lane CSI configuration rather than the 2-lane one the Pi 4 Model B uses. It’s worth noting that both device trees share a lot of copy-and-paste DNA (the Zero 3 W even has a duplicated “PWR_GPIO” line name), so I wouldn’t read too much into either of those until we see an actual board. I’d love to see PCIe exposed on a Zero, but I’m not holding my breath.

The second surprise is a Raspberry Pi 4 Model A . We haven’t had a Model A since the Raspberry Pi 3 Model A+ back in 2018, and the formula has always been the same: take the Model B, strip out the bits most people can live without (RJ45, some USB ports etc), and knock a chunk off the price. The Pi 4 Model A looks to follow that recipe pretty closely, though the price comment may not quite hold. Let’s see!

The device tree doesn’t tell us anything about USB. On the Model B, the USB 3 ports made use of the PCIe bus, and the PCIe controller is enabled here too, so USB 3 is possible, but the 3 Model A+ only had a single USB-A port and I’d probably expect the same here.

Here’s a quick side-by-side of what the device trees tell us, with the Pi 4 Model B thrown in for good measure. Anything marked with an asterisk is my interpretation of the device tree rather than something it states outright.

Quite a lot, I’m afraid. Device trees don’t describe RAM, so there’s no word on memory configurations, and there’s nothing on pricing, clock speeds, connector types or a release date either.

Pricing is the big one for me. Memory costs haven’t exactly been kind lately (I covered the last round of increases alongside the 1GB Raspberry Pi 5 launch ), and a lower-cost Pi 4 variant makes a lot of sense in that context. The BCM2711 is a mature chip at this point, it’s well supported in software, and a cut-down board gives people who don’t need a Pi 5 something cheaper to reach for. The Zero 3 W is a tougher one to call though, as the Zero range has always lived and died by its price, and I can’t imagine the BCM2711 being as cheap to build around as the RP3A0.

On the whole, I like what I’m seeing here. The Zero 3 W looks like the upgrade a lot of people have been asking for since the Zero 2 W landed, and the 4 Model A feels like a sensible way of squeezing more life out of the Pi 4 platform at a time when components aren’t getting any cheaper. The external antenna support on the 4 Model A is a really nice touch if it makes it to the final board.

Saying that, everything above comes from device tree files rather than an official spec sheet, so mileage may vary when the real thing turns up. Kernel support landing ahead of launch is usually a good sign that it’s not far off, and you can bet I’ll be throwing both the Zero 3 W and the 4 Model A onto sbc.compare as soon as I can get one in my hands.

Which of the two are you more excited about? Do let me know in the comments!

Related posts: Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W vs Zero W Benchmarks – Pi Zero Showdown – 1GB Raspberry Pi 5 Launched Alongside Price Increases

Bret has worked with Raspberry Pi computers for almost 10 years now and in that time he's benchmarked and tested over 30 Single Board computers. In his day job, he's a systems administrator for a large cloud computing provider.
